factual_problem: Misleading wording, not wrong doctrine: 'a rule or process the organisation imposes' sits next to the item 'A firewall filtering inbound traffic by rule'. A learner matching words would move the firewall to Administrative. 'logic running in software or hardware' could also pull the hardware lock on the server-room door toward Technical. Also, 'what an attacker would have to defeat' fits administrative controls badly: nobody 'defeats' a signed AUP or a background check, an insider just ignores it or a candidate lies to get through it.
reason: Restates the three-way definition (logical, administrative, physical) as an enforcer test. Applying it still needs the concept for every item. No item gets placed by keyword alone, and the only word overlap ('rule') points the wrong way.

factual_problem: Under the old ISC2 Code guidance (dropped from the current Code), 'take care to be truthful, objective, cautious, and within your competence' sat under Canon II. Under that reading the competence-disclosure item could defensibly go to II. The hint states the III reading as settled. Canon III's old guidance ('render only those services for which you are fully competent') supports III, so the item is not wrong, but the hint should not be the thing that settles a genuinely two-sided item.
reason: Not a pure method. It is built around the exact shape of particular items: 'an honest act that is part of serving the people who hired you' matches only one item, telling a client up front that the work is beyond your qualifications, and sends it to III. 'Looking after the profession' steers the honest-reporting item (the peer selling exam questions) to IV. A learner who doesn't know the canons can pull both items out of II just by spotting 'honest act + client' or 'honest act + profession'. It also implies by elimination that the sales-pitch and authorisation items stay in II. That narrows about four of the eight items, more than a hint that only states the II/III boundary would.

Only points at the Identify step coming before Assess ('before you could compare it'). Identify-first is obvious without any hint, since you can't rank something you haven't described, and so is Assess-before-Choose. The hint pins nothing the learner wouldn't already place, and it gives no help on the only non-obvious pair (Apply vs Document residual). Close to a hint that costs q for nothing, which the standing rule warns against.

factual_problem: Not a hint problem but a sequence assumption: if the chosen treatment is 'accept' (or 'transfer' or 'avoid'), there is no control to apply, so the single fixed order quietly assumes 'mitigate'. Consider wording the Apply step as 'Implement the chosen treatment and verify it'.
reason: A method (order by when the audit evidence could first exist). It does help with the one genuinely non-obvious pair, verification evidence before the residual-risk sign-off, but only for a learner who knows that residual risk is what remains after the control is in place. The obvious steps (Identify first, Assess before Choose) need no help. No keyword shortcut.

factual_problem: The test misfires on 'Data at rest must be encrypted with AES-256'. AES-256 is an algorithm, not a product, so it plausibly survives replacing every technology next year, and the test then pushes a Standard toward Policy. The same goes for 'approved hardened OS image', which survives a platform change if the image is simply rebuilt. The tech-independent vs tech-specific idea is right; the 'replace every technology' wording is what leaks ambiguity. Suggest something like 'would it need rewriting if the organisation changed products, algorithms or settings?'.
reason: States the defining Policy/Standard distinction: a policy is tech-agnostic, a standard names the specific thing. It doesn't separate Standard from Procedure, or Guideline from Law. There is a weak surface shortcut (items without technical nouns go higher), but it only works if you already know the hierarchy order. That is concept, not a bypass.
